statement: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that standardizes integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools.

MCP's stated purpose is to give applications a standardized way to share contextual information with language models, expose tools and capabilities to AI systems, and build composable integrations and workflows.
The authoritative protocol requirements of MCP are defined by the TypeScript schema (schema.ts), which is the normative source of truth an implementation must conform to.

The RFC-2119 / BCP-14 requirement keywords (MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, OPTIONAL, etc.) carry their normative BCP-14 meaning only when written in all capitals.
condition: the keyword appears in all uppercase letters in the document

statement: MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 messages as its wire format to establish communication between participants.

MCP defines three participant roles: Hosts (LLM applications that initiate connections), Clients (connectors living inside the host application), and Servers (services that provide context and capabilities).
In MCP, the Host is the LLM application that initiates connections, and Clients are the connectors within the host that maintain those connections.
MCP connections are stateful, so implementations must maintain per-connection session state rather than treating each message as independent.
The MCP base protocol requires server and client capability negotiation, so peers must agree on supported features before using them.

Servers can offer three feature types to clients: Resources (context and data for the user or the AI model), Prompts (templated messages and workflows for users), and Tools (functions the AI model can execute).
Resources are the MCP feature for exposing context and data intended for use by the user or the AI model.
Prompts are the MCP feature for exposing templated messages and workflows intended for users.
Tools are the MCP feature that exposes functions for the AI model to execute.

Clients can offer three feature types to servers: Sampling (server-initiated agentic behaviour and recursive LLM interactions), Roots (server-initiated inquiries into URI or filesystem boundaries), and Elicitation (server-initiated requests for additional information from users).
Sampling is the client-offered feature that lets a server initiate agentic behaviour and recursive LLM interactions.
MCP includes cross-cutting utility mechanisms for configuration, progress tracking, cancellation, error reporting, and logging.
MCP enables powerful capabilities through arbitrary data access and code-execution paths, which creates security and trust risks that every implementor must deliberately address.
Users must explicitly consent to, and understand, all data access and operations performed on their behalf.
Users must retain control over what data is shared and what actions are taken.
Implementors should provide clear user interfaces for reviewing and authorizing activities.
A host must obtain explicit user consent before exposing any user data to a server.
A host must not transmit resource data elsewhere without user consent.
User data should be protected with appropriate access controls.
Because tools represent arbitrary code execution, they must be treated with appropriate caution.
Descriptions of tool behaviour, such as annotations, should be treated as untrusted unless they come from a server the user already trusts.
exception: the tool behaviour description is obtained from a trusted server

statement: A host must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool.
Users should be able to understand what each tool does before authorizing its use.
Users must explicitly approve any LLM sampling request before it is executed.
Users should be able to control whether sampling occurs at all, the actual prompt that will be sent, and what results the server is allowed to see.
MCP intentionally limits a server's visibility into the prompts used during sampling.
MCP cannot enforce its security principles at the protocol level, so responsibility for consent, authorization, access control, and privacy falls on the implementor.

Implementors should build robust consent and authorization flows, document security implications clearly, implement appropriate access controls and data protections, follow security best practices, and consider privacy implications in their feature designs.
condition: the security principle cannot be enforced by the protocol itself

statement: MCP follows a client-host-server architecture in which each host process can run multiple client instances.
The client-host-server separation exists to preserve clear security boundaries and to isolate concerns between integrated components.
MCP is built on JSON-RPC as its underlying message format.
MCP is a stateful session protocol whose focus is context exchange and sampling coordination between clients and servers.
The host process acts as the container and coordinator for all client instances.
The host is responsible for creating and managing the lifecycle of its client instances.
The host controls client connection permissions and lifecycle.
The host enforces security policies and consent requirements.
The host handles user authorization decisions.
The host coordinates AI/LLM integration and sampling.
The host manages aggregation of context across its multiple clients.
Each client is created by the host and maintains a single isolated connection to one server.
Each client maintains a 1:1 relationship with a particular server, establishing one stateful session per server.
The client handles protocol negotiation and capability exchange with its server.
The client routes protocol messages bidirectionally between host and server.
The client manages subscriptions and notifications for its server connection.
The client maintains security boundaries between the servers it connects to.
Servers expose resources, tools, and prompts to clients via MCP primitives.
Servers operate independently, each with a focused set of responsibilities.
Servers request sampling through the client interface rather than directly.
Servers must respect the security constraints imposed by the host.
A server may be implemented either as a local process or as a remote service.
Servers should be extremely easy to build: complex orchestration is handled by the host application, leaving servers to focus on specific, well-defined capabilities.
Servers should be highly composable, each providing focused functionality in isolation so that multiple servers can be combined seamlessly over the shared protocol.
A server must not be able to read the whole conversation nor see into other servers.
A server should receive only the contextual information necessary for its task; the full conversation history stays with the host.
Each server connection is isolated and cross-server interactions are controlled exclusively by the host.
Features can be added to servers and clients progressively: the core protocol provides minimal required functionality and additional capabilities are negotiated as needed.
Servers and clients can evolve independently while backwards compatibility is maintained.
MCP uses a capability-based negotiation system in which clients and servers explicitly declare their supported features during initialization.
The capabilities negotiated at initialization determine which protocol features and primitives are available for the duration of that session.
Both clients and servers must respect the declared capabilities throughout the session.
Additional capabilities beyond the negotiated set can be introduced through extensions to the protocol.
A server must advertise every implemented server feature in its declared capabilities.
A server may emit resource subscription notifications only if it has declared subscription support in its capabilities.
condition: the server has declared subscription support

statement: A client may invoke a tool only if the server has declared the corresponding tool capability.
condition: the server has declared tool capabilities

statement: A server may request sampling only if the client has declared sampling support in its capabilities.
condition: the client has declared sampling support

statement: MCP is organized into modular layers — base protocol, lifecycle management, authorization, server features, client features, and utilities — so implementations support exactly the features they need while separating concerns.
Every MCP implementation MUST support the base protocol and lifecycle-management components.
MCP components beyond base protocol and lifecycle (authorization, server features, client features, utilities) MAY be implemented selectively based on the application's needs.
All messages exchanged between MCP clients and servers MUST conform to the JSON-RPC 2.0 specification.
An MCP request MUST include an id that is either a string or an integer.
An MCP request id MUST NOT be null, in contrast to base JSON-RPC which permits it.
A requestor MUST NOT reuse a request id that it has already used earlier in the same session.
condition: within the same session

statement: A result response MUST carry the same id as the request it answers.
A result response MUST include a result field.
The result field of a response MAY take any JSON object structure.
An error response MUST include the same id as its request, except when a malformed request prevents the id from being read.
exception: the request is malformed and the id cannot be read

statement: An error response MUST include an error field that contains both a code and a message.
Error codes MUST be integers.
The receiver of a notification MUST NOT send any response to it, because notifications are one-way messages.
A notification MUST NOT include an id.
Implementations using an HTTP-based transport SHOULD conform to the MCP authorization specification.
condition: HTTP-based transport

statement: Implementations using the STDIO transport SHOULD NOT follow the MCP authorization specification and should instead retrieve credentials from the environment.
condition: STDIO transport

statement: Clients and servers MAY negotiate their own custom authentication and authorization strategies.
The TypeScript schema is the authoritative source of truth for all MCP protocol messages and structures.
The JSON Schema is generated automatically from the TypeScript source of truth for use with automated tooling.
When a schema omits a $schema field, implementations MUST treat it as JSON Schema 2020-12 (the default dialect).
condition: the schema has no explicit $schema field

statement: A schema MAY include a $schema field to declare a dialect other than the default.
Implementations MUST support at least JSON Schema 2020-12 and SHOULD document which additional dialects they support.
Implementors are RECOMMENDED to use JSON Schema 2020-12.
Clients and servers MUST validate schemas according to the schema's declared or default dialect.
Implementations MUST handle unsupported schema dialects gracefully by returning an error that indicates the dialect is not supported.
condition: the declared dialect is unsupported

statement: Schemas MUST be valid according to their declared or default dialect.
The _meta property is reserved by MCP, and implementations MUST NOT make assumptions about the values stored at MCP-reserved _meta keys.
A _meta key prefix, when present, MUST be a series of dot-separated labels ending in a slash, where each label starts with a letter and ends with a letter or digit.
condition: a prefix is specified on the _meta key

statement: Any _meta key prefix whose second label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp is reserved for MCP use.
Implementations SHOULD use reverse-DNS notation for _meta key prefixes.
A non-empty _meta key name MUST begin and end with an alphanumeric character.
condition: the name segment is non-empty

statement: Each Icon object MUST include a src URI, which is either an HTTP/HTTPS URL or a data URI pointing to the icon resource.
Clients that render icons MUST support at least the image/png and image/jpeg MIME types.
condition: the client renders icons

statement: Clients that render icons SHOULD additionally support image/svg+xml and image/webp.
condition: the client renders icons

statement: Consumers of icon metadata MUST treat both the metadata and the icon bytes as untrusted input and defend against network, privacy, and parsing risks.
Icon URIs MUST use an HTTPS or data: scheme; clients MUST reject unsafe schemes such as javascript:, file:, ftp:, or ws: and disallow scheme changes or redirects to hosts on different origins.
Icons MUST be fetched without credentials — no cookies, Authorization headers, or client credentials.
To resist resource-exhaustion attacks, consumers should guard against oversized images, large dimensions, or excessive frames and MAY set limits on image and content size.
Consumers SHOULD exercise caution when rendering icons that may carry executable content (for example SVG with embedded JavaScript) and MAY sanitize or disallow specific file types before rendering.
Consumers MUST validate icon MIME types and file contents by detecting content type via magic bytes, rejecting on mismatch or unknown type, and maintaining a strict allowlist of image types.
The MCP client-server connection lifecycle consists of three ordered phases: initialization, operation, and shutdown.
The initialization phase exists to negotiate capabilities and agree on a protocol version before normal communication begins.
The initialization phase must be the first interaction between an MCP client and server.
During initialization the client and server establish protocol-version compatibility, exchange and negotiate capabilities, and share implementation details.
The client must initiate initialization by sending an initialize request.
The client's initialize request must include the protocol version it supports, its capabilities, and its implementation information.
The server must respond to an initialize request with its own capabilities and implementation information.
After initialization succeeds, the client must send an initialized notification to signal it is ready for normal operations.
Before the server has responded to the initialize request, the client should not send any requests other than pings.
exception: pings are permitted before the initialize response

statement: Before receiving the initialized notification, the server should not send any requests other than pings and logging messages.
exception: pings and logging are permitted before the initialized notification

statement: In the initialize request the client must send a protocol version that it supports.
The protocol version the client proposes should be the latest version the client supports.
If the server supports the client's requested protocol version, the server must respond with that same version.
condition: the server supports the client's requested protocol version

statement: If the server does not support the client's requested protocol version, the server must respond with another protocol version that it does support.
condition: the server does not support the requested protocol version

statement: The alternative protocol version a server proposes should be the latest version the server supports.
condition: the server must offer an alternative version

statement: If the client does not support the protocol version returned in the server's response, the client should disconnect.
condition: the client does not support the version in the server's response

statement: Over HTTP, the client must include the MCP-Protocol-Version header carrying the negotiated version on all requests after initialization.
condition: the transport is HTTP

statement: Negotiated client and server capabilities determine which optional protocol features are available for the session.
Client-side capabilities advertised at initialization include roots, sampling, elicitation, tasks, and experimental features.
Server-side capabilities advertised at initialization include prompts, resources, tools, logging, completions, tasks, and experimental features.
The listChanged sub-capability signals support for list-change notifications for prompts, resources, and tools.
The subscribe sub-capability signals support for subscribing to individual item changes and applies to resources only.
condition: resources capability

statement: During the operation phase the client and server exchange messages according to the capabilities negotiated at initialization.
During operation both parties must respect the protocol version that was negotiated.
During operation both parties must use only the capabilities that were successfully negotiated.
During shutdown one side, usually the client, cleanly terminates the protocol connection.
MCP defines no dedicated shutdown messages; connection termination is signalled through the underlying transport instead.
For the stdio transport the client should initiate shutdown by first closing its input stream to the server child process.
condition: the transport is stdio

statement: For stdio shutdown, if the server does not exit within a reasonable time after its input is closed, the client should send SIGTERM.
condition: the transport is stdio and the server has not exited within a reasonable time

statement: For stdio shutdown, if the server does not exit within a reasonable time after SIGTERM, the client should send SIGKILL.
condition: the transport is stdio and the server has not exited within a reasonable time after SIGTERM

statement: Under stdio the server may initiate shutdown by closing its output stream to the client and exiting.
condition: the transport is stdio

statement: For HTTP transports, shutdown is signalled by closing the associated HTTP connection(s).
condition: the transport is HTTP

statement: Implementations should set timeouts on all sent requests to prevent hung connections and resource exhaustion.
When a request has not received a success or error response within its timeout, the sender should issue a cancellation notification for that request and stop waiting.
condition: the timeout elapses without a response

statement: SDKs and middleware should allow request timeouts to be configured on a per-request basis.
Implementations may reset a request's timeout clock when they receive a progress notification for that request, since it indicates work is ongoing.
condition: a progress notification is received for the request

statement: Implementations should always enforce a maximum timeout regardless of progress notifications, to bound the impact of a misbehaving peer.
Implementations should be prepared to handle protocol-version mismatch, failure to negotiate required capabilities, and request timeouts.
An unsupported-protocol-version error is reported with JSON-RPC error code -32602 and data listing the supported and requested versions.
MCP encodes all protocol messages using JSON-RPC, and those JSON-RPC messages MUST be UTF-8 encoded.
MCP defines two standard transports — stdio and Streamable HTTP — and clients SHOULD support stdio whenever possible.
Clients and servers MAY implement additional custom, pluggable transports; the protocol is transport-agnostic and can run over any channel supporting bidirectional message exchange.
In the stdio transport the client launches the MCP server as a subprocess that reads JSON-RPC messages from its stdin and writes messages to its stdout.
Over stdio, messages MUST be delimited by newlines and MUST NOT contain embedded newlines.
Over stdio the server MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message, and the client MUST NOT write anything to the server's stdin that is not a valid MCP message.
Over stdio the server MAY write UTF-8 log strings to stderr, and the client MAY capture, forward, or ignore that stderr and SHOULD NOT assume stderr output indicates error conditions.
In Streamable HTTP the server is an independent process handling multiple client connections and MUST expose a single MCP endpoint path that supports both HTTP POST and GET.
Streamable HTTP servers MAY use Server-Sent Events (SSE) to stream multiple server messages over HTTP.
Streamable HTTP servers MUST validate the Origin header on all incoming connections to prevent DNS rebinding attacks.
If the Origin header is present and invalid, the server MUST respond with HTTP 403 Forbidden.
condition: the Origin header is present and invalid

statement: When running locally, Streamable HTTP servers SHOULD bind only to localhost (127.0.0.1) rather than all network interfaces (0.0.0.0).
condition: the server is running locally

statement: Streamable HTTP servers SHOULD implement proper authentication for all connections.
Every JSON-RPC message the client sends MUST be a new HTTP POST request to the MCP endpoint.
On each POST the client MUST include an Accept header listing both application/json and text/event-stream as supported content types.
The body of a POST request MUST be a single JSON-RPC request, notification, or response.
When the POST body is a JSON-RPC response or notification, the server MUST return HTTP 202 Accepted with no body if it accepts the input, or an HTTP error status (e.g. 400 Bad Request) if it cannot.
condition: the POST body is a JSON-RPC response or notification

statement: When the POST body is a JSON-RPC request, the server MUST respond with either Content-Type text/event-stream (opening an SSE stream) or Content-Type application/json (one JSON object), and the client MUST support both cases.
condition: the POST body is a JSON-RPC request

statement: When the server opens an SSE stream it SHOULD immediately send an SSE event carrying an event ID and an empty data field to prime the client to reconnect using that ID as Last-Event-ID.

The server MAY close an SSE connection without terminating the stream to avoid long-lived connections; when it does so before terminating the stream it SHOULD first send an SSE retry field, the client SHOULD then poll by reconnecting, and the client MUST respect the retry delay before reconnecting.
An SSE stream SHOULD eventually include the JSON-RPC response for the request sent in the POST body, and after that response is sent the server SHOULD terminate the SSE stream.
Before sending the JSON-RPC response, the server MAY send JSON-RPC requests and notifications on the stream, and those messages SHOULD relate to the originating client request.
A disconnection SHOULD NOT be interpreted as the client cancelling its request; to cancel, the client SHOULD explicitly send an MCP CancelledNotification.
The client MAY issue an HTTP GET (including an Accept header listing text/event-stream) to open a server-to-client SSE stream without first sending data via POST.
In response to a client GET the server MUST either return Content-Type text/event-stream or return HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed indicating it offers no SSE stream at that endpoint.
On a GET-initiated SSE stream the server MUST NOT send a JSON-RPC response unless it is resuming a stream associated with a previous client request.
exception: resuming a stream associated with a previous client request

statement: The server MUST send each JSON-RPC message on only one connected stream and MUST NOT broadcast the same message across multiple streams.

Servers MAY attach an id field to SSE events, and when present that event ID MUST be globally unique across all streams within the session (or across all streams with that client when session management is not in use).
condition: the server attaches an id field to SSE events

statement: SSE event IDs SHOULD encode enough information to identify the originating stream so the server can correlate a Last-Event-ID header to the correct stream, acting as a per-stream cursor.

To resume after a disconnection the client SHOULD issue an HTTP GET to the MCP endpoint including the Last-Event-ID header; resumption is always via HTTP GET with Last-Event-ID regardless of how the original stream was initiated.
When replaying messages on resume, the server MUST NOT replay messages that would have been delivered on a different stream.
condition: the server replays messages after a Last-Event-ID on resume

statement: A Streamable HTTP server MAY assign a session ID by including it in an MCP-Session-Id header on the InitializeResult response; that session ID SHOULD be globally unique and cryptographically secure and MUST contain only visible ASCII characters (0x21 to 0x7E).

When the server has returned a session ID, the client MUST include it in the MCP-Session-Id header on all subsequent requests, and a server that requires a session ID SHOULD respond with HTTP 400 Bad Request to requests other than initialization that lack the header.
condition: the server returned a session ID at initialization

statement: The server MAY terminate a session at any time, after which it MUST respond with HTTP 404 Not Found to requests bearing that session ID; on receiving such a 404 the client MUST start a new session by sending a new InitializeRequest with no session ID attached.
condition: the server has terminated the session

statement: A client that no longer needs a session SHOULD send an HTTP DELETE to the MCP endpoint with the MCP-Session-Id header to explicitly terminate it, and the server MAY respond with HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed to refuse client-initiated termination.
When using HTTP the client MUST include the MCP-Protocol-Version header on all subsequent requests to the server, and that value SHOULD be the version negotiated during initialization.

If the server receives no MCP-Protocol-Version header and cannot otherwise identify the version it SHOULD assume protocol version 2025-03-26, and if it receives an invalid or unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version it MUST respond with HTTP 400 Bad Request.
condition: the server receives a missing, invalid, or unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version header

statement: To maintain backwards compatibility with the deprecated HTTP+SSE transport, servers wanting to support older clients should continue hosting both the old SSE and POST endpoints alongside the new Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint.

A client supporting older servers should POST an InitializeRequest to the server URL, and if that fails with HTTP 400, 404, or 405 it should fall back by issuing a GET expecting an SSE stream whose first event is an endpoint event, indicating the server runs the old HTTP+SSE transport.
condition: the InitializeRequest POST fails with 400, 404, or 405

statement: Implementers of custom transports MUST preserve the JSON-RPC message format and lifecycle requirements defined by MCP, and SHOULD document their connection-establishment and message-exchange patterns to aid interoperability.
The Model Context Protocol supports optional cancellation of in-progress requests through notification messages, and either side of the connection may initiate it.
To cancel an in-progress request, a party sends a `notifications/cancelled` notification whose params carry the `requestId` of the request to cancel and an optional `reason` string.
The `reason` string in a cancellation notification is optional and is intended only to be logged or displayed, not to alter protocol behaviour.
A cancellation notification MUST only reference a request that was previously issued in the same direction as the notification.
A cancellation notification MUST only reference a request that the sender believes is still in-progress.
Clients MUST NOT cancel the `initialize` request.
For task-augmented requests, the dedicated `tasks/cancel` request MUST be used instead of the `notifications/cancelled` notification.
condition: the request is a task-augmented request

statement: The `tasks/cancel` mechanism is distinct from `notifications/cancelled` because it returns the final task state.
On receiving a valid cancellation notification, receivers SHOULD stop processing the cancelled request.
On receiving a valid cancellation notification, receivers SHOULD free the resources associated with the cancelled request.
After cancelling a request, receivers SHOULD NOT send a response for that cancelled request.
Receivers MAY ignore a cancellation notification when the referenced request is unknown, has already completed, or cannot be cancelled.
exception: the referenced request is unknown, already completed, or cannot be cancelled

statement: The sender of a cancellation notification SHOULD ignore any response to the cancelled request that arrives after the notification was sent.
Because of network latency, a cancellation notification may arrive after the target request has finished processing and even after its response has already been sent.
Both parties MUST handle cancellation race conditions gracefully, since a cancellation may arrive after processing has completed.
Both parties SHOULD log cancellation reasons to aid debugging.
Application user interfaces SHOULD indicate when cancellation has been requested.
Invalid cancellation notifications SHOULD be ignored, including those with unknown request IDs, references to already-completed requests, or malformed content.
exception: the notification has an unknown request ID, references an already-completed request, or is malformed

statement: Ignoring invalid or racing cancellation notifications preserves the intended fire-and-forget nature of notifications while tolerating race conditions in asynchronous communication.
The Model Context Protocol provides an optional ping mechanism that lets either party verify that its counterpart is still responsive and the connection is alive.
Either the client or the server can initiate a ping by sending a `ping` request.
Ping is implemented as a simple request/response pattern rather than a dedicated protocol subsystem.
A ping request is a standard JSON-RPC 2.0 request whose `method` is `ping` and which carries no parameters.
The receiver of a ping MUST respond promptly with an empty JSON-RPC result (`result: {}`).
The ping response reuses the same JSON-RPC `id` as the originating ping request so sender and reply can be correlated.
When no ping response is received within a reasonable timeout period, the sender MAY consider the connection stale, terminate the connection, or attempt reconnection procedures.
condition: no response is received within a reasonable timeout period

statement: Implementations SHOULD periodically issue pings to detect connection health.
The frequency of pings SHOULD be configurable.
Ping timeouts SHOULD be chosen appropriately for the network environment.
Excessive pinging SHOULD be avoided in order to reduce network overhead.
Ping timeouts SHOULD be treated as connection failures.
Multiple failed pings MAY trigger a connection reset.
condition: multiple consecutive ping failures occur

statement: Implementations SHOULD log ping failures for diagnostics.
The Model Context Protocol provides optional progress tracking for long-running operations via notification messages.
Either party in an MCP exchange may send progress notifications to report an operation's status.
A party that wants to receive progress updates for a request must include a progressToken in that request's `_meta` metadata.
condition: the party wants to receive progress updates for the request

statement: A progressToken must be either a string or an integer value.
A progressToken must be unique across all of the sender's active requests.
The sender may pick a progressToken by any means it chooses, so long as it is unique across active requests.
condition: the token is unique across all active requests

statement: The receiver may send progress notifications carrying the original progressToken, the current progress value, and optionally a total value and a message.
The progress value must increase with each notification, even when the total is unknown.
The progress value and the total value may be floating-point numbers.
The message field should provide relevant human-readable progress information.
A progress notification must reference only a token that was supplied in an active request and is associated with an in-progress operation.
A receiver may choose not to send any progress notifications for a request.
A receiver may send progress notifications at whatever frequency it judges appropriate.
A receiver may omit the total value when the total is unknown.
condition: the total is unknown

statement: For a task-augmented request, the progressToken from the original request must keep being used for progress notifications throughout the task's lifetime, including after the CreateTaskResult has been returned.
condition: the request is task-augmented

statement: A task's progressToken remains valid and bound to the task until the task reaches a terminal status.
condition: the request is task-augmented

statement: Progress notifications for a task must use the same progressToken that was supplied in the initial task-augmented request.
condition: the request is task-augmented

statement: Progress notifications for a task must stop after the task reaches a terminal status of completed, failed, or cancelled.
condition: the request is task-augmented

statement: Both senders and receivers should track their active progress tokens.
Both parties should implement rate limiting on progress notifications to prevent flooding.
Progress notifications must stop after the operation completes.

An MCP task is a durable state machine that wraps the execution state of a task-augmented request and exists for requestor polling and deferred result retrieval; each task is uniquely identified by a receiver-generated task ID.
The tasks feature was introduced in MCP version 2025-11-25 and is experimental, so its design and behaviour may change in future protocol versions.
Either a client or a server can act as the requestor (sender of a task-augmented request) or the receiver (executor of the task); tasks are not restricted to one direction.

The task model is requestor-driven: requestors are responsible for augmenting requests with tasks and polling for results, while receivers control which request types support task augmentation and manage task lifecycles.
The protocol does not mandate any specific user-interaction model for tasks; implementations may expose tasks through any interface pattern.
A server or client that supports task-augmented requests MUST declare a `tasks` capability during initialization, structured by request category with boolean properties per supported request type.
A requestor SHOULD only augment a request with a task when the receiver has declared the corresponding `tasks` capability for that request type.
condition: the receiver has declared the corresponding tasks capability

statement: If `capabilities.tasks` is not defined by a peer, the other party SHOULD NOT attempt to create tasks on requests to it.
condition: capabilities.tasks is not defined

statement: The set of capabilities under `capabilities.tasks.requests` is exhaustive: any request type not listed there does not support task augmentation.
Tools individually declare task support in the `tools/list` result via `execution.taskSupport`, whose value may be `required`, `optional`, or `forbidden`.
If a server's capabilities do not include `tasks.requests.tools.call`, clients MUST NOT attempt task augmentation on that server's tools regardless of any `execution.taskSupport` value.
condition: server capabilities omit tasks.requests.tools.call
exception: the tool-level execution.taskSupport value is ignored in this case

statement: When `tasks.requests.tools.call` is supported, a tool whose `execution.taskSupport` is absent or `forbidden` MUST NOT be invoked as a task, and the server SHOULD return `-32601` (Method not found) if a client tries; this is the default behaviour.
condition: tasks.requests.tools.call is supported and execution.taskSupport is absent or forbidden

statement: When a tool's `execution.taskSupport` is `optional`, clients MAY invoke it either as a task or as a normal request; when it is `required`, clients MUST invoke it as a task and the server MUST return `-32601` (Method not found) if they do not.

Task-augmented requests follow a two-phase response pattern: the receiver immediately returns a `CreateTaskResult` containing task data, and the actual operation result becomes available later through `tasks/result` after the task completes.
To create a task, a requestor includes the `task` field in the request params and MAY include a `ttl` (milliseconds) indicating the desired task lifetime from creation.
A `CreateTaskResult` contains only task data and does not include the actual operation result.

A server MAY supply an `io.modelcontextprotocol/model-immediate-response` key in the `CreateTaskResult` `_meta` to give the model an immediate placeholder result while a task runs; this guidance is non-binding and provisional and may change in future versions.
Requestors poll for completion by sending `tasks/get` requests and SHOULD respect the `pollInterval` value returned in responses when choosing polling frequency.

Requestors SHOULD continue polling via `tasks/get` until the task reaches a terminal status (`completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`) or reaches `input_required`; invoking `tasks/result` does not by itself mean polling should stop.

The `tasks/result` operation returns exactly what the underlying request would have returned, and its result structure matches the original request type (for example `CallToolResult` for `tools/call`).
A `tasks/result` request blocks until the task reaches a terminal status, but the requestor MAY continue polling via `tasks/get` in parallel when not actively blocked waiting for the result.
Receivers MAY send a `notifications/tasks/status` notification when a task's status changes, carrying the full task state so the requestor need not make an extra `tasks/get` call.
Requestors MUST NOT rely on receiving `notifications/tasks/status` notifications because they are optional, and SHOULD continue polling via `tasks/get` to ensure they see status updates.
condition: the notification is optional and may not be sent

statement: A receiver that does not declare the task capability for a request type MUST process such requests normally and ignore any task-augmentation metadata that is present.
condition: the receiver has not declared the task capability for that request type

statement: A receiver that declares the task capability for a request type MAY reject non-task-augmented requests of that type, effectively requiring task augmentation.
condition: the receiver declares the task capability for that request type

statement: Task IDs MUST be string values, MUST be generated by the receiver when creating a task, and MUST be unique among all tasks controlled by that receiver.
A task MUST begin in the `working` status when created.

Receivers MUST only follow valid status transitions: from `working` to `input_required`, `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`; from `input_required` to `working`, `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`; and a task in a terminal status (`completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`) MUST NOT transition to any other status.

When a receiver needs input from the requestor to complete a task, it SHOULD move the task to `input_required`, MUST include the `io.modelcontextprotocol/related-task` metadata in the resulting request, and SHOULD transition the task out of `input_required` (typically back to `working`) once all required input is received.
condition: the receiver needs additional input from the requestor to complete the task

statement: When a requestor observes the `input_required` status, it SHOULD preemptively call `tasks/result` to receive the pending input request.
condition: the task is in input_required status

statement: Receivers MUST include ISO 8601 `createdAt` and `lastUpdatedAt` timestamps in all task responses, indicating when the task was created and last updated.
Receivers MAY override a requestor's requested `ttl`, and MUST report the actual `ttl` duration (or `null` for unlimited) in `tasks/get` responses.
After a task's `ttl` lifetime has elapsed, receivers MAY delete the task and its results regardless of the task's status.
condition: the task's ttl lifetime has elapsed

statement: Receivers MAY include a `pollInterval` (milliseconds) in `tasks/get` responses to suggest polling frequency, and requestors SHOULD respect it when provided.
A receiver that accepts a task-augmented request MUST return a `CreateTaskResult` as the response, and SHOULD return it as soon as possible after accepting the task.

For a `tasks/result` request on a task in a terminal status, the receiver MUST return the underlying request's final result, whether a successful result or a JSON-RPC error; for a task still in `working` or `input_required`, the receiver MUST block the response until the task reaches a terminal status.

All requests, notifications, and responses related to a task MUST include the `io.modelcontextprotocol/related-task` key in their `_meta`, with a `taskId` matching the associated task ID, so dependent messages (e.g. an elicitation) share the task's ID.

For the `tasks/get`, `tasks/result`, and `tasks/cancel` operations the `taskId` request parameter is the source of truth; requestors SHOULD NOT include `io.modelcontextprotocol/related-task` metadata in these requests and receivers MUST ignore it if present.
condition: the operation is tasks/get, tasks/result, or tasks/cancel
exception: the taskId is already carried in the request/response structure

statement: For task listing, receivers SHOULD use cursor-based pagination and MUST include a `nextCursor` when more tasks are available; requestors MUST treat cursors as opaque tokens; and any task retrievable via `tasks/get` for a requestor MUST also be retrievable via `tasks/list` for that requestor.
Receivers MUST reject cancellation of a task already in a terminal status with error code `-32602` (Invalid params).
condition: the target task is already in a terminal status

statement: On a valid cancellation request the receiver SHOULD attempt to stop execution and MUST transition the task to `cancelled` before responding; once cancelled the task MUST remain `cancelled` even if execution later completes or fails.

Receivers MAY delete a cancelled task at any time (including immediately), so requestors SHOULD NOT rely on cancelled tasks being retained and should retrieve any needed information before cancelling.
condition: the task has been cancelled

statement: Task-augmented requests support progress notifications, and the `progressToken` supplied in the initial request remains valid throughout the task's lifetime.
A task's state comprises `taskId`, `status`, an optional `statusMessage`, `createdAt`, `ttl`, `pollInterval`, and `lastUpdatedAt`.

The defined task statuses are `working` (processing), `input_required` (receiver needs requestor input), `completed` (succeeded, results available), `failed` (did not complete successfully, including a tool call whose result has `isError` true), and `cancelled` (cancelled before completion).
The `tasks/result` operation MUST include the `io.modelcontextprotocol/related-task` metadata in its response, because the result structure itself does not otherwise carry the task ID.
condition: the operation is tasks/result

statement: For `tasks/get`, `tasks/list`, and `tasks/cancel`, requestors and receivers SHOULD NOT include the `io.modelcontextprotocol/related-task` metadata, since the `taskId` is already present in the message structure.
condition: the operation is tasks/get, tasks/list, or tasks/cancel

statement: Tasks use two distinct error-reporting mechanisms: standard JSON-RPC protocol errors for protocol-level issues, and task execution errors surfaced through the task status.

Receivers MUST return `-32602` (Invalid params) for protocol errors such as an invalid or nonexistent `taskId` in `tasks/get`, `tasks/result`, or `tasks/cancel`; an invalid or nonexistent cursor in `tasks/list`; or an attempt to cancel a task already in a terminal status.
Receivers MUST return `-32603` (Internal error) for internal errors.
A receiver MAY return `-32600` (Invalid request) when it receives a non-task-augmented request but requires task augmentation for that request type.
condition: the receiver requires task augmentation for that request type

statement: Receivers SHOULD provide informative error messages describing the cause of an error.
Receivers are not required to retain tasks indefinitely; it is compliant to return a 'task not found' error for a task whose expired state has been purged.
condition: the task has expired and been purged

statement: When the underlying request does not complete successfully the task moves to `failed` status — this includes JSON-RPC errors during execution and, for tool calls, a tool result with `isError` set to true — and the `tasks/get` response SHOULD include a `statusMessage` with diagnostic information about the failure.

On `tasks/result` for a terminal task, if the underlying request produced a JSON-RPC error the receiver MUST return that same error, and if it completed successfully the receiver MUST return a successful response containing that result.

Task IDs are the primary mechanism for accessing task state and results, so without proper access controls any party that guesses or obtains a task ID could access sensitive information or manipulate tasks it did not create.
When an authorization context is provided, receivers MUST bind tasks to that context.
condition: an authorization context is provided

statement: When context-binding is available, receivers MUST reject `tasks/get`, `tasks/result`, and `tasks/cancel` for tasks that do not belong to the requestor's authorization context, and MUST ensure `tasks/list` returns only tasks in the requestor's context.
condition: context-binding is available

statement: When context-binding is unavailable, receivers SHOULD clearly document that task results may be accessible to any requestor able to guess the task ID.
condition: context-binding is unavailable

statement: When context-binding is unavailable, receivers MUST generate cryptographically secure task IDs with enough entropy to prevent guessing, and should consider using shorter TTL durations to reduce the exposure window.
condition: context-binding is unavailable

statement: Receivers that cannot identify requestors SHOULD NOT declare the `tasks.list` capability, because listing would expose task metadata to any requestor regardless of task-ID entropy.
condition: the receiver cannot identify requestors

statement: Receivers SHOULD implement rate limiting on task operations to prevent denial-of-service and enumeration attacks.

For resource management, receivers SHOULD enforce limits on concurrent tasks per requestor and maximum `ttl` durations, clean up expired tasks promptly, document the maximum supported `ttl` and concurrent-task limits, and implement monitoring and alerting for resource usage.

For audit purposes, receivers SHOULD log task creation, completion, and retrieval events, include the auth context in logs when available, and monitor for suspicious patterns such as many failed task lookups or excessive polling.
Requestors SHOULD log task lifecycle events for debugging and audit and track task IDs together with their associated operations.
MCP elicitation lets a server request additional information from the user by going through the client, keeping the client in control of user interaction and data sharing.

Elicitation offers two modes: form mode for in-band structured data collection (with an optional JSON schema for validation) and URL mode for out-of-band interactions that must not pass through the client.
Servers must not use form mode to request sensitive secrets or credentials such as passwords, API keys, access tokens, or payment credentials.
Servers must use URL mode for any interaction that involves sensitive information (secrets or credentials that grant access or authorize transactions).
condition: the interaction involves sensitive secrets or credentials

statement: Requesting general contact or profile data (name, email, username) via form mode is permitted at the server's discretion, subject to the user's ability to review and decline; it is not categorically prohibited the way secrets are.
exception: the data is a secret or credential granting access or authorizing transactions

statement: Clients must present UI that clearly identifies which server is requesting the information.
Clients must respect user privacy and offer clear options to decline and to cancel an elicitation.
In form mode, clients must let users review and modify their responses before those responses are sent.
condition: the elicitation is form mode

statement: In URL mode, clients must clearly display the target domain or host and obtain user consent before navigating to the URL.
condition: the elicitation is URL mode

statement: A client that supports elicitation must declare the elicitation capability during initialization.
An empty elicitation capability object is, for backwards compatibility, equivalent to declaring support for form mode only.
A client declaring the elicitation capability must support at least one mode, form or url.
Servers must not send an elicitation request using a mode the client has not declared support for.

A server requests user information by sending an elicitation/create request that must include a mode (optional for form, defaulting to form if omitted) and a human-readable message explaining why the interaction is needed.
For backwards compatibility a server may omit the mode field for form mode, and clients must treat any request lacking a mode field as a form mode request.
condition: the request is form mode

statement: A form mode elicitation request must set mode to form (or omit mode) and include a requestedSchema giving the JSON Schema of the expected response.
condition: the elicitation is form mode

statement: Form mode requestedSchema is restricted to a flat object of primitive properties (string, number/integer, boolean, enum); nested structures, arrays of objects beyond enums, and other advanced JSON Schema features are intentionally unsupported to keep the client UX simple.
Form mode string schemas support the formats email, uri, date, and date-time.
Clients that support default values should pre-populate form fields with the schema's declared defaults.
condition: the client supports defaults and the schema declares them

statement: URL mode elicitation was introduced in the 2025-11-25 version of the MCP specification and its design may change in future protocol revisions.
A URL mode elicitation request must specify mode url, include a message, and include a url parameter plus a unique elicitationId.
condition: the elicitation is URL mode

statement: The url parameter of a URL mode request must contain a valid URL.

URL mode elicitation is not a mechanism for authorizing the client's access to the server (that is MCP authorization); it is for the server to obtain sensitive information or third-party authorization on the user's behalf, and the client's bearer token stays unchanged.
A server may send a notifications/elicitation/complete notification when a URL-mode out-of-band interaction finishes.
When sending a completion notification the server must send it only to the client that initiated the elicitation and must include the elicitationId from the original request.
Clients must ignore completion notifications that reference an unknown or already-completed elicitationId.
Clients should still provide manual retry and cancel controls in case a completion notification never arrives.

When a request cannot proceed until an elicitation completes, a server may return URLElicitationRequiredError (code -32042), and it must not return this error except when URL mode elicitation is actually required.
condition: the request cannot be processed until a URL mode elicitation completes

statement: A URLElicitationRequiredError must list the elicitations that must complete before retry, and every listed elicitation must be URL mode and carry an elicitationId.
Elicitation responses use a three-action model, accept, decline, or cancel, applicable to both form and URL modes.

On accept in form mode the response content holds the submitted data matching the requested schema, whereas on accept in URL mode the content field is omitted; decline and cancel typically omit content.

A URL mode accept means the user consented to the interaction, not that the interaction is complete; the interaction happens out of band and the client only learns the outcome if the server sends a completion notification.
Servers implementing elicitation must securely associate collected state with individual users, following the security best-practices guidance.
Elicitation state must not be associated with session IDs alone, and state storage must be protected against unauthorized access.
For remote MCP servers, user identity for elicitation state must, where possible, be derived from credentials obtained via MCP authorization (for example the sub claim).
condition: the server is a remote MCP server and authorization credentials are available

statement: Collecting sensitive credentials through URL mode keeps them out of the LLM context, the MCP client, and any intermediate servers, reducing the risk of exposure through client-side logging or other attack vectors.
A server must not rely on URL mode elicitation to authorize users for itself; external third-party authorization via URL mode is separate from MCP authorization.
Third-party credentials obtained via URL mode elicitation must never transit through or be transmitted to the MCP client, preserving the security boundary.
A server must not reuse the client's credentials for the third-party service, because that is forbidden token passthrough.
The user must authorize the MCP server directly for third-party access, in an interaction that occurs outside the MCP protocol and does not involve the client.
The MCP server is responsible for securely storing and managing third-party tokens bound to the user's identity, which means it must be stateful.

Servers must return -32042 (URLElicitationRequiredError) when a request cannot be processed until an elicitation completes, and clients must return -32602 (Invalid params) when a server sends an elicitation/create using a mode the client did not declare.
Servers must bind each elicitation request to the client and to the user identity.
Clients should implement user-approval controls, allow users to decline an elicitation at any time, and apply rate limiting.
Clients should present each elicitation so it is clear what information is being requested and why.
Servers must not put sensitive end-user information such as credentials or PII into the URL sent in a URL elicitation request.
Servers must not provide a URL that is pre-authenticated to access a protected resource, since that URL could be used by a malicious client to impersonate the user.
Servers should not include clickable URLs in any field of a form mode elicitation request, and should use HTTPS URLs outside development environments.
condition: the environment is non-development (for HTTPS)

statement: Clients must not automatically pre-fetch a URL-mode URL or any of its metadata.
Clients must not open a URL-mode URL without explicit user consent and must show the user the full URL for examination before consent.

Clients must open the server-provided URL in a way that prevents the client or LLM from inspecting the page content or the user's inputs (for example iOS SFSafariViewController rather than WKWebView).
Clients should highlight the URL's domain to mitigate subdomain spoofing and warn on ambiguous or suspicious URIs such as those containing Punycode.
Clients should not render URLs as clickable in any elicitation field except the url field of a URL elicitation request.

Servers must not treat client-provided user identification as authoritative without server-side verification, because such identity claims can be forged; they should identify the user via authorization instead.
Clients should validate elicitation responses against the provided schema, and servers should validate that received data matches the requested schema.

Because a URL mode URL can be forwarded by an attacker to a victim, the server must verify the identity of whoever opens the URL before accepting any information, typically via the MCP authorization server (e.g. a session cookie).

To prevent a cross-user phishing account-takeover, the server must ensure the user who started the elicitation is the same user who completes the authorization flow, and this identity mechanism must be resilient to an attacker modifying the elicitation URL.

A common mitigation is a server-hosted connect URL (e.g. /connect?elicitationId=...) that confirms the opening user matches the elicitation's user (for instance by comparing the session cookie's subject to the authorization server's sub claim) before redirecting to the third-party authorization endpoint.
MCP defines a standardized mechanism for clients to expose filesystem 'roots' to servers, where each root marks a directory or file boundary constraining where a server may operate.
A server can query a supporting client for its current list of roots and can be notified when that list subsequently changes.

Roots are usually surfaced to users through workspace or project configuration interfaces, such as a directory/file picker optionally combined with automatic workspace detection from version control or project files.
The protocol mandates no particular user-interaction model for roots; an implementation may expose them through whatever interface pattern suits it.
A client that supports roots must declare the `roots` capability during protocol initialization.
condition: the client supports roots

statement: The `roots` capability carries a `listChanged` boolean that indicates whether the client will emit notifications when its root list changes.
A server retrieves the current roots by sending a `roots/list` JSON-RPC request to the client.
The `roots/list` response returns a `roots` array in which each entry is a root object carrying a `uri` and an optional `name`.
A client that supports `listChanged` must send a `notifications/roots/list_changed` notification whenever its set of roots changes.
condition: the client advertised listChanged support

statement: The expected root-change flow is: the client emits a list_changed notification and the server responds by re-issuing `roots/list` to obtain the updated set.
A root's `uri` field must be a `file://` URI under the current specification version.
exception: a future specification version may permit other URI schemes

statement: A root's `name` field is an optional human-readable label intended only for display.
A client should reply with the standard JSON-RPC error `-32601` (method not found) when it does not support roots, and `-32603` for internal errors.
condition: a roots request fails for one of these reasons

statement: A client must only expose roots for which the appropriate permissions exist.
A client must validate every root URI to prevent path-traversal attacks.
A client must implement proper access controls over the roots it exposes.
A client must monitor the ongoing accessibility of the roots it has exposed.
A server should handle the case where a previously exposed root becomes unavailable.
A server should respect root boundaries during its operations.
A server should validate all filesystem paths it uses against the roots provided by the client.
A client should obtain user consent before exposing roots to a server.
A client should provide a clear user interface for managing roots.
A client should verify a root's accessibility before exposing it to a server.
A client should monitor for changes to its roots.
A server should check for the roots capability before attempting to use roots.
condition: before invoking roots functionality

statement: A server should handle changes to the root list gracefully.
A server should respect root boundaries in its operations.
A server should cache root information appropriately rather than re-fetching it unnecessarily.

MCP sampling provides a standardized way for servers to request LLM completions from language models via the client, so the client retains control over model access, selection, and permissions and servers need no API keys of their own.
Through sampling a server can request text, audio, or image-based interactions and may optionally include context from MCP servers in its prompts.
Sampling lets servers implement agentic behaviour by allowing LLM calls to occur nested inside other MCP server features.
The protocol does not mandate any specific user-interaction model; implementations may expose sampling through whatever interface pattern suits them.
For trust, safety, and security there should always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny a sampling request.
Applications should provide UI that makes reviewing sampling requests easy and intuitive.
Applications should let users view and edit prompts before they are sent to the model.
Applications should present generated responses for user review before they are delivered.
Servers can request that the client's LLM use tools during sampling by supplying a tools array and an optional toolChoice configuration in the sampling request.
A client must declare support for tool use via the sampling.tools capability in order to receive tool-enabled sampling requests.
A server must not send tool-enabled sampling requests to a client that has not declared the sampling.tools capability.
condition: the target client has not declared sampling.tools

statement: A client that supports sampling must declare the sampling capability during initialization.
Basic sampling is declared with the capability object {"sampling": {}}; tool-use support adds a nested tools object and context-inclusion support adds a nested context object.
The includeContext parameter values 'thisServer' and 'allServers' are soft-deprecated and may be removed in a future spec release.

Servers should avoid the soft-deprecated includeContext values (for example by omitting includeContext, which defaults to 'none') and should not use them unless the client has declared the sampling.context capability.
exception: the client has declared the sampling.context capability

statement: To request a language-model generation a server sends a sampling/createMessage request over JSON-RPC.
A sampling/createMessage request carries params including messages, optional modelPreferences (hints, intelligencePriority, speedPriority), an optional systemPrompt, and maxTokens.
A createMessage result returns the assistant role, the generated content, the model that was used, and a stopReason.
To enable tool use a server includes a tools array (each tool having a name, description, and inputSchema) and optionally a toolChoice in the createMessage request.
When the LLM returns tool_use content the result carries stopReason 'toolUse', and the assistant content is an array of tool_use blocks each with an id, name, and input.
In the multi-turn tool loop the server executes the requested tools, sends a new sampling request with the tool results appended, receives the next response, and repeats until done.
A server may cap the maximum number of tool-loop iterations, and can pass toolChoice {mode: 'none'} on the final iteration to force a final text result.
When a user message contains tool results (type 'tool_result') it must contain only tool results; mixing tool results with text, image, or audio content in the same message is not allowed.
condition: the user message contains one or more tool_result blocks

statement: Restricting tool-result messages to tool results alone keeps them compatible with provider APIs that use dedicated roles for tool results, such as OpenAI's 'tool' role and Gemini's 'function' role.

Every assistant message containing ToolUseContent blocks must be immediately followed by a user message consisting entirely of ToolResultContent blocks, with each tool use matched by a tool result whose toolUseId equals the tool use's id, before any other message.
condition: tool use is being used in sampling

statement: Requiring each tool use to be resolved by a matching tool result before continuing ensures tool uses are always resolved first, lets provider APIs process multiple tool uses in parallel, and keeps a consistent request-response pattern.
MCP messages use only two roles, 'user' and 'assistant'; tool-use requests are returned with the assistant role and tool results are sent back with the user role.

toolChoice mode 'auto' lets the model decide whether to use tools and is the default, 'required' forces the model to use at least one tool before completing, and 'none' forbids the model from using any tools.
MCP allows a model to issue multiple tool-use requests in parallel by returning an array of ToolUseContent, and Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini all support parallel tool use natively.

Exposing the ability to disable parallel tool use (for providers that support it, e.g. OpenAI's parallel_tool_calls: false) is an optional implementation extension and is not part of the core MCP specification.
Sampling messages can carry text content, image content (base64 data plus mimeType), or audio content (base64 data plus mimeType).
Model preferences abstract model selection because servers and clients may use different providers, so a server cannot reliably request a specific model by name.

Capability priorities are three normalized 0-to-1 values: costPriority (higher prefers cheaper models), speedPriority (higher prefers faster models), and intelligencePriority (higher prefers more capable models).

Model hints are treated as flexible substrings of model names, are evaluated in order of preference, are advisory only, and clients may map them to equivalent models from a different provider while making the final model selection themselves.

Clients should return errors for common failures: user rejected the sampling request (code -1), a tool result is missing in the request (-32602 Invalid params), and tool results were mixed with other content (-32602 Invalid params).

For security, clients should implement user-approval controls, should respect model-preference hints, and should implement rate limiting; both parties should validate message content and must handle sensitive data appropriately.

When tools are used in sampling a server must ensure that every ToolUseContent item is answered by a ToolResultContent item with a matching toolUseId and that the responding user message contains only tool results, and both parties should enforce iteration limits on tool loops.
condition: tools are used in sampling

statement: MCP servers add context to language models by exposing primitives that mediate interactions between clients, servers, and models.
An MCP server exposes exactly three server primitives: prompts, resources, and tools.
Prompts are pre-defined templates or instructions that guide language-model interactions.
Prompts are user-controlled: they are interactive templates invoked by explicit user choice, such as slash commands or menu options.
Resources are structured data or content that provide additional context to the model.
Resources are application-controlled: they are contextual data attached and managed by the client, such as file contents or git history.
Tools are executable functions that let models perform actions or retrieve information.
Tools are model-controlled: they are functions exposed to the LLM so it can take actions, such as issuing API POST requests or writing files.
Each MCP primitive has a distinct control owner: prompts are user-controlled, resources are application-controlled, and tools are model-controlled.
The Model Context Protocol provides a standardized way for servers to expose prompt templates that clients can discover, retrieve, and customize with arguments.
MCP prompts are designed to be user-controlled: they are exposed from servers to clients with the intent that the user explicitly selects them for use.
Prompts are typically triggered through user-initiated commands in the client user interface, such as slash commands, so users can discover and invoke them.
The protocol does not mandate any specific user-interaction model; implementors may expose prompts through any interface pattern that suits their needs.
A server that supports prompts MUST declare the `prompts` capability during initialization.
condition: the server supports prompts

statement: The `prompts.listChanged` capability flag indicates whether the server will emit notifications when the list of available prompts changes.
To retrieve available prompts, a client sends a `prompts/list` request, and this operation supports pagination via a cursor.
A `prompts/list` response returns a `prompts` array and an optional `nextCursor` for paginating to the next page of results.
To retrieve a specific prompt, a client sends a `prompts/get` request naming the prompt and supplying its arguments.
Prompt arguments may be auto-completed through the completion API.
A server that declared the `listChanged` capability SHOULD send a `notifications/prompts/list_changed` notification when the list of available prompts changes.
condition: the server declared the listChanged capability and the prompt list changed

statement: A prompt definition includes a unique `name` identifier and optional `title`, `description`, `icons`, and `arguments` fields.
A prompt message contains a `role` of either "user" or "assistant" and a `content` field of one of the supported content types.
Prompt message content may be one of four types: text, image, audio, or embedded resource.
All prompt-message content types support optional annotations carrying metadata about audience, priority, and modification times.
Image content in a prompt message MUST be base64-encoded and include a valid MIME type.
condition: the message carries image content

statement: Audio content in a prompt message MUST be base64-encoded and include a valid MIME type.
condition: the message carries audio content

statement: An embedded resource in a prompt message MUST include a valid resource URI, the appropriate MIME type, and either text content or base64-encoded blob data.
condition: the message embeds a server-side resource

statement: A server SHOULD return the standard JSON-RPC error -32602 (Invalid params) for an invalid prompt name or for missing required arguments.
A server SHOULD return the standard JSON-RPC error -32603 (Internal error) for internal failures.
A server SHOULD validate prompt arguments before processing them.
A client SHOULD handle pagination when retrieving large prompt lists.
Both client and server SHOULD respect capability negotiation for prompts.
Implementations MUST carefully validate all prompt inputs and outputs to prevent injection attacks and unauthorized access to resources.
MCP resources are application-driven: the host application decides how to incorporate a server's resources as model context based on its own needs.

The MCP protocol does not mandate any specific user-interaction model for exposing resources; implementations may use any interface pattern (e.g. explicit picker, search/filter, or heuristic/model-driven automatic inclusion).
Every MCP resource is uniquely identified by a URI (per RFC3986).
A server that supports resources MUST declare the `resources` capability during initialization.
condition: the server exposes resources at all

statement: The `resources` capability exposes two independently optional features, `subscribe` and `listChanged`; a server may support neither, either, or both.
The `subscribe` feature indicates the client can subscribe to be notified of changes to individual resources.
The `listChanged` feature indicates the server will emit a notification when the set of available resources changes.
Clients discover available resources by sending a `resources/list` request, which supports cursor-based pagination.
Clients retrieve resource contents by sending a `resources/read` request carrying the target resource `uri`.
Servers can expose parameterized resources as resource templates using RFC6570 URI templates, discovered via a `resources/templates/list` request.
Resource-template arguments may be auto-completed through the MCP completion API.
A server that declared the `listChanged` capability SHOULD send a `notifications/resources/list_changed` notification when its resource list changes.
condition: the server declared the listChanged capability

statement: Clients may subscribe to a specific resource with `resources/subscribe` and then receive a `notifications/resources/updated` notification whenever that resource changes.
condition: the server supports the subscribe feature

statement: After receiving an `updated` notification for a subscribed resource, the client re-reads the resource (via `resources/read`) to obtain the new contents.
A resource definition requires a `uri` and a `name`; `title`, `description`, `icons`, `mimeType`, and `size` are optional fields.
Resource contents carry either text (a `text` field) or binary data (a base64-encoded `blob` field), not both in the same content entry.
Resources, resource templates, and content blocks support optional annotations that hint to clients how to use or display the resource.
The `audience` annotation is an array over the values `user` and `assistant`, declaring the intended audience(s) of a resource.
The `priority` annotation is a number from 0.0 to 1.0 where 1 means effectively required (most important) and 0 means entirely optional (least important).
The `lastModified` annotation is an ISO 8601 timestamp indicating when the resource was last modified.
Clients can use resource annotations to filter by intended audience, prioritize which resources to include in context, and sort or display resources by modification recency.
Servers SHOULD use the `https://` URI scheme only when the client can fetch and load the resource directly from the web itself, without reading it through the MCP server.
condition: the client can fetch and load the resource directly from the web on its own

statement: For resources the client cannot fetch directly, servers SHOULD prefer another or a custom URI scheme rather than `https://`, even when the server itself downloads the content over the internet.
condition: the resource is not directly web-fetchable by the client

statement: The `file://` scheme identifies filesystem-like resources, but such resources need not map to an actual physical filesystem.
Servers MAY tag a `file://` resource with an XDG MIME type (e.g. `inode/directory`) to represent non-regular files such as directories that lack a standard MIME type.
condition: representing a non-regular file such as a directory

statement: The `git://` scheme is defined for Git version-control integration.
The list of standard URI schemes is non-exhaustive: implementations may define additional custom schemes, but custom schemes MUST conform to RFC3986.
For common failures servers SHOULD return standard JSON-RPC errors, using code -32002 for resource-not-found and -32603 for internal errors.
A resource-not-found error SHOULD include the offending `uri` in its `data` field to aid the client.
Security: MCP servers MUST validate all resource URIs.
Security: access controls SHOULD be implemented for sensitive resources.
Security: binary resource data MUST be properly encoded.
Security: resource permissions SHOULD be checked before performing resource operations.
MCP tools are model-controlled: a language model discovers and invokes them automatically from contextual understanding and the user's prompts.
The protocol does not mandate any specific user-interaction pattern; implementations may expose tools through any interface that suits their needs.
For trust, safety, and security there should always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations.
Applications should provide UI that makes clear which tools are exposed to the model and should show clear visual indicators when tools are invoked.
Applications should present confirmation prompts to the user for operations, to ensure a human remains in the loop.
Servers that support tools must declare the `tools` capability.
The `listChanged` capability flag indicates whether the server will emit notifications when its available tool list changes.
Clients discover available tools by sending a `tools/list` request.
The `tools/list` operation supports pagination via an optional cursor parameter.
Clients invoke a tool by sending a `tools/call` request that names the tool and supplies its arguments.
A server that declared the `listChanged` capability should send a `notifications/tools/list_changed` notification when its tool list changes.
condition: only when the server declared the listChanged capability

statement: A tool's `inputSchema` must be a valid JSON Schema object and must not be null.
Tool `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` default to JSON Schema draft 2020-12 when no `$schema` field is present.
For a tool with no parameters the recommended `inputSchema` is `{"type":"object","additionalProperties":false}`, which explicitly accepts only empty objects.
Clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.
condition: annotations originate from a server
exception: unless the annotations come from a trusted server

statement: Tool names should be between 1 and 128 characters in length, inclusive.
Tool names should be considered case-sensitive.
Tool names should use only ASCII letters, digits, underscore, hyphen, and dot, and should not contain spaces, commas, or other special characters.
Tool names should be unique within a server.
A tool result may contain structured content, unstructured content, or both.
Unstructured tool-result content is returned in the `content` field and may hold multiple items of differing types (text, image, audio, resource link, embedded resource).
Structured tool-result content is returned as a JSON object in the `structuredContent` field of the result.
A tool that returns structured content should also return the serialized JSON in a text content block for backwards compatibility.
When a tool provides an output schema, servers must return structured results that conform to that schema.
condition: when the tool declares an output schema

statement: When a tool provides an output schema, clients should validate the structured results against that schema.
condition: when the tool declares an output schema

statement: A tool may return resource links (a URI the client can fetch or subscribe to) for extra context, but such links are not guaranteed to appear in a `resources/list` result.
Servers that use embedded resources in tool results should implement the `resources` capability.
condition: when the server embeds resources in tool results

statement: Tools report errors via two mechanisms: JSON-RPC protocol errors and tool execution errors flagged with `isError: true` in the tool result.
Protocol errors cover unknown tools, malformed requests, and server errors, whereas tool execution errors cover API failures, input-validation errors, and business-logic errors.
Clients should provide tool execution errors to language models so the model can self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters.
Clients may provide protocol errors to language models, though these are less likely to result in successful recovery.
Servers must validate all tool inputs.
